# Abstract {.unnumbered}

::: {.abstract-box}
**Aim.** The Asian longhorned tick, *Haemaphysalis longicornis*, is a vector of pathogens of
veterinary and public-health importance and has been invasive in Australia and New Zealand for more
than a century. We estimated current climatic suitability for the species across both countries
using a model selected explicitly for its ability to transfer between regions.

**Location.** Global calibration across the native range (East Asia) and invaded ranges (North
America and Oceania); projection to Australia and New Zealand.

**Methods.** We modelled 389 spatially thinned, regionally stratified occurrence records with
MaxEnt. To correct for strongly uneven sampling effort, we used a target-group background
normalised within each region and allocated among regions in proportion to area. Ten *a priori*
predictor sets and their MaxEnt settings were evaluated by leave-one-region-out (LORO) and
spatial-block cross-validation, prioritising low omission of withheld records. The selected
configurations of the three best-performing predictor sets were combined into a consensus model. We
mapped suitability, extrapolation, bootstrap uncertainty, limiting factors and suitable areas far
from known records, and compared climatic niches between ranges with ecospat.

**Results.** Only predictor sets containing annual mean temperature transferred reliably between
regions. A set derived by automated variance-inflation-factor (VIF) selection, which lacked an
absolute temperature variable, ranked sites well within a withheld region but under-predicted
suitability there: when Oceania was withheld, it omitted every Oceanian record. The consensus model transferred well
(mean LORO AUC = 0.86, continuous Boyce index = 0.81). Trained without any Oceanian records, it
predicted the Australian and New Zealand distribution well (AUC = 0.91, Boyce = 0.94). Suitable
climate covers about 669,000 km² (8.3% of the two countries): the eastern Australian seaboard from
south-east Queensland to Victoria, Tasmania, a small area of south-western Western Australia and
almost all of New Zealand. Aridity and large diurnal temperature ranges limit the species inland;
high temperatures limit it in the north. About 208,000 km² of suitable climate lies more than 100 km
from any known record, mostly in Tasmania, the South Island of New Zealand and western Victoria.
The Oceanian niche was equivalent to, and more similar than expected to, the native niche
(Schoener's *D* = 0.47). The recently invaded North American range occupies a small fraction of the
native niche (unfilling = 0.96).

**Main conclusions.** The climatic niche of *H. longicornis* has been conserved during invasion of
Australia and New Zealand, so native-range information transfers well to these countries, provided
models include an absolute temperature gradient and correct for regional sampling imbalance.
Climatically suitable but unrecorded areas, particularly Tasmania and southern New Zealand, are
priorities for targeted surveillance.
:::

**Keywords:** *Haemaphysalis longicornis*; Asian longhorned tick; species distribution model; MaxEnt; model transferability; niche shift; biosecurity; Australia; New Zealand

# Introduction

The Asian longhorned tick, *Haemaphysalis longicornis* Neumann, is a three-host ixodid tick native
to temperate East Asia: eastern China, the Korean Peninsula, Japan and the Russian Far East
[@hoogstraal1968; @zhao2020]. It parasitises a wide range of mammals and birds and is of
considerable veterinary and public-health importance. It transmits *Theileria orientalis*,
including the Ikeda genotype responsible for outbreaks of oriental theileriosis in Australian cattle
[@kamau2011], and in East Asia it is a principal vector of severe fever with thrombocytopenia
syndrome virus [@yu2011] and many other pathogens [@zhao2020]. The species exists as bisexual and
parthenogenetic populations. Because a single parthenogenetic female can found a population, the
parthenogenetic form has spread far beyond the native range [@hoogstraal1968]. It has long been
established in eastern Australia, New Zealand and several south-west Pacific islands, where it is
an important pest of livestock [@heath2016]. Since its detection in New Jersey in 2017 it has spread
rapidly across the eastern United States [@rainey2018].

Correlative species distribution models (SDMs) are the main tool for estimating where an invasive
species could establish, and several have been developed for *H. longicornis*, mostly to forecast
its spread in North America [@raghavan2019; @rochlin2019; @namgyal2020]. Using such models to
predict suitability in an invaded region raises three well-known problems. First, presence-only
records reflect sampling effort as much as occurrence, and uncorrected sampling bias distorts both
fitted responses and predicted distributions [@phillips2009]. Second, a model is only useful for
an invaded region if the species–climate relationship it learns transfers across space. This is
not guaranteed when invaded populations occupy climates not used in the native range (niche
expansion) or fail to occupy climates used there (unfilling) [@guisan2014; @petitpierre2012].
Third, complex models and automated variable selection can produce over-fitted response surfaces
that interpolate well but extrapolate poorly [@radosavljevic2014; @elith2010; @owens2013].
Despite this, transferability is rarely evaluated directly, and most SDMs are assessed with random
or spatial cross-validation within the calibration area [@wenger2012; @roberts2017].

*H. longicornis* is a good case for addressing these issues. It has been recorded across three
continents spanning both hemispheres, which allows transfer to be tested explicitly by withholding
entire regions. The Australian and New Zealand populations are long-established, and the species'
distribution there is reasonably well documented, which provides a strong test of whether a
globally calibrated model reproduces a known invaded range. For Australia and New Zealand, the
practical questions are where climate currently permits the tick to persist, which climatic factors
limit its spread inland and northward, and which climatically suitable areas lack records and so
merit surveillance.

Here we develop a MaxEnt model for *H. longicornis* calibrated across its native and invaded ranges
and use it to map current climatic suitability across Australia and New Zealand. Our specific aims
were to: (i) correct for strongly uneven sampling effort among regions using a region-balanced
target-group background; (ii) select predictors and model complexity explicitly for transferability
among regions; (iii) map current suitability, extrapolation risk, uncertainty and limiting climatic
factors across Australia and New Zealand; (iv) quantify niche overlap and niche dynamics between the
native and invaded ranges; and (v) identify suitable but unrecorded areas as candidate targets for
surveillance.

# Methods

## Occurrence data

Occurrence records of *H. longicornis* were compiled from the Global Biodiversity Information
Facility (GBIF), the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA), a global literature compilation of North
American and Pacific records [@rochlin2019] and a georeferenced dataset of ticks in China
[@zhang2019]. Records without coordinates and duplicate localities were removed and the remaining
records were spatially thinned to a minimum inter-record distance of 10 km to reduce spatial
autocorrelation. Because East Asian records dominated the thinned dataset (61%), records were then
geographically stratified so that no single region contributed more than 35% of records (random
subsampling of the over-represented region only). Each record was assigned to a calibration region:
East Asia (native range; China, Japan, the Korean Peninsula, the Russian Far East, plus a single
Himalayan record), North America (invaded; eastern USA) or Oceania (invaded; Australia, New
Zealand and Pacific islands). These upstream steps are implemented in Steps 1–2 of the analysis
pipeline (`code_2/`), and the resulting dataset is the starting point here.

```{r}
#| label: load-occ
occ <- read_csv(file.path(proc_v2, "occurrences_with_climate.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(region = if_else(region == "Other", "East_Asia", region))   # Himalayan record -> native range

world10 <- ne_countries(scale = 10, returnclass = "sf")
occ_sf  <- st_as_sf(occ, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)
occ$country <- world10$admin[st_nearest_feature(occ_sf, world10)]

# All available environmental layers (WorldClim 2.1 bioclim, ENVIREM, CHELSA VPD), 2.5 arcmin
env_all <- rast(file.path(proc_v2, "env_all_global.tif"))
cand_vars <- c(paste0("bio", c(1:7, 10:17)), "pet_idx", "aridity_idx", "cmi_idx", "vpd_annual")
n_occ <- nrow(occ); n_by_reg <- table(occ$region)
```

## Environmental predictors

Candidate predictors were the WorldClim 2.1 bioclimatic variables at 2.5 arc-minute resolution
[@fick2017], three ENVIREM moisture variables (annual potential evapotranspiration, Thornthwaite
aridity index and climatic moisture index) [@title2018], and mean annual vapour-pressure deficit
(VPD) from CHELSA v2.1 (1981–2010), aggregated from 30 arc-seconds to the WorldClim grid
[@karger2017]. BIO8, BIO9, BIO18 and BIO19 were excluded a priori because they combine temperature
and precipitation quarters and produce known spatial discontinuities, leaving
`r length(cand_vars)` candidate variables.

## Accessible area and background

The accessible area (*M*) [@barve2011] was defined as the union of 1,000-km buffers around all
occurrence records, clipped to land. This encompasses the areas plausibly reachable through
livestock movement, wildlife hosts and migratory birds, while excluding the distant and
environmentally irrelevant regions that inflate discrimination metrics. *M* was partitioned into the
three calibration regions by assigning each grid cell to the region of its nearest occurrence record.

Presence records of *H. longicornis* reflect where people have looked for ticks as much as where the
tick occurs. To account for this we used a target-group background [@phillips2009]. Target-group
records comprised all georeferenced Ixodidae records on GBIF within *M* plus the tick survey records
of @zhang2019, de-duplicated at 0.1°. Because GBIF tick records are overwhelmingly North American,
a single global sampling-effort surface would place almost all background points in North America.
We therefore (i) built the sampling-effort surface separately within each region, using a Gaussian
kernel (σ = 1°, about 100 km) on 0.25° record counts, normalised to a maximum of 1 within each region
with a floor of 0.02 so that unsurveyed areas remain available; and (ii) allocated the 10,000
background points among regions in proportion to each region's land area within *M*. Within regions,
points were drawn with probability proportional to sampling effort × cell area. A second,
independent set of 10,000 points was drawn uniformly (area-weighted) across *M* and used only for
model evaluation, so that all candidate models were evaluated against a common reference
distribution of available environments.

```{r}
#| label: accessible-area-background
M_r <- rast(file.path(proc_v2, "env_selected_M.tif"))[[1]]
M_r <- classify(!is.na(M_r), cbind(0, NA)); names(M_r) <- "M"

# Region membership of each M cell (nearest occurrence), computed at 0.25 deg then disaggregated
M6  <- aggregate(M_r, 6, fun = "max", na.rm = TRUE)
xy6 <- as.data.frame(M6, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)[, 1:2]
reg6 <- match(occ$region[st_nearest_feature(st_as_sf(xy6, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 4326), occ_sf)], regs)
reg_r6 <- rast(M6); reg_r6[cellFromXY(reg_r6, as.matrix(xy6))] <- reg6
reg_r  <- mask(resample(reg_r6, M_r, method = "near"), M_r); names(reg_r) <- "region"

cells  <- which(!is.na(values(reg_r)))
c_reg  <- values(reg_r)[cells]
c_area <- values(cellSize(reg_r, unit = "km"))[cells]
reg_area  <- tapply(c_area, c_reg, sum)
reg_share <- reg_area / sum(reg_area)
n_bg  <- 10000
n_reg <- round(n_bg * reg_share)

# Target-group records (GBIF Ixodidae within M + Zhang et al. 2019 Chinese tick records)
tg_gbif  <- read_csv(file.path(proc_v2, "ixodidae_points.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
tg_zhang <- read_csv(file.path(base_dir, "data", "Zhang_et_al_2019_ms_dataset_v1.csv"),
                     show_col_types = FALSE) |> filter(!is.na(lon), !is.na(lat)) |> dplyr::select(lon, lat)
tg <- bind_rows(tg_gbif, tg_zhang) |>
  mutate(lon_b = round(lon, 1), lat_b = round(lat, 1)) |>
  distinct(lon_b, lat_b, .keep_all = TRUE) |> dplyr::select(lon, lat)
tg$region <- occ$region[st_nearest_feature(st_as_sf(tg, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326), occ_sf)]

# Region-normalised kernel sampling-effort surface
tg_cnt <- rasterize(as.matrix(tg[, c("lon", "lat")]), M6, fun = "count", background = 0)
tg_kde <- focal(tg_cnt, focalMat(tg_cnt, 1, "Gauss"), fun = "sum", na.rm = TRUE)
tg_kde <- resample(tg_kde, M_r, method = "bilinear")
kv <- values(tg_kde)[cells]; kv[is.na(kv)] <- 0
bias <- numeric(length(cells))
for (r in seq_along(regs)) { i <- c_reg == r; bias[i] <- pmax(kv[i] / max(kv[i]), 0.02) }
bias_r <- rast(reg_r); bias_r[cells] <- bias; names(bias_r) <- "bias"

sample_bg <- function(prob, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  idx <- unlist(lapply(seq_along(regs), function(r) {
    i <- which(c_reg == r); sample(i, n_reg[r], prob = prob[i] * c_area[i]) }))
  xy <- xyFromCell(reg_r, cells[idx])
  bind_cols(tibble(lon = xy[, 1], lat = xy[, 2], region = regs[c_reg[idx]]),
            terra::extract(env_all, xy)) |> drop_na(all_of(cand_vars))
}
bg_train   <- sample_bg(bias, 102)                       # bias-corrected training background
bg_uniform <- sample_bg(rep(1, length(cells)), 101)      # uniform background (sensitivity analysis)
bg_eval    <- sample_bg(rep(1, length(cells)), 999)      # independent evaluation background

writeRaster(bias_r, file.path(proc_v3, "bias_surface_regional.tif"), overwrite = TRUE)
write_csv(bg_train, file.path(proc_v3, "background_train.csv"))
write_csv(bg_eval,  file.path(proc_v3, "background_eval.csv"))
```

## Variable selection

Collinearity was assessed across the accessible area (on the evaluation background), not at
occurrence points, because collinearity among predictors in the environments available to the
species is what affects coefficient estimation and transfer [@dormann2013]. Rather than relying on
automated stepwise variance-inflation-factor (VIF) elimination, which can discard ecologically
critical variables, we defined ten candidate predictor sets *a priori*. Each set contained four or
five variables spanning the axes known to constrain the off-host survival and development of
ixodid ticks: thermal regime or thermal limits, temperature variability, moisture supply, and
desiccation stress [@needham1991; @heath2016]. All sets satisfied |Spearman's ρ| ≤ 0.75 and VIF < 5
across *M* (@supptbl-sets). Set A reproduces the predictors selected by stepwise VIF reduction in an
earlier iteration of this analysis and contains no absolute temperature variable. Each candidate set
was evaluated over a grid of MaxEnt settings (see below) and the set containing the best-ranked
configurations were carried forward (see below).

```{r}
#| label: candidate-sets
cand_sets <- list(
  A = c("bio2", "bio3", "bio13", "aridity_idx", "vpd_annual"),
  B = c("bio5", "bio6", "bio13", "bio17", "aridity_idx"),
  C = c("bio1", "bio2", "bio12", "bio15", "aridity_idx"),
  D = c("bio2", "bio5", "bio6", "bio13", "aridity_idx"),
  E = c("vpd_annual", "bio4", "bio13", "bio17", "aridity_idx"),
  F = c("bio5", "bio6", "bio12", "bio15", "aridity_idx"),
  G = c("bio1", "bio2", "bio13", "bio17", "aridity_idx"),
  H = c("bio1", "bio12", "bio15", "aridity_idx"),
  I = c("bio10", "bio2", "bio12", "bio15", "aridity_idx"),
  J = c("bio11", "bio2", "bio12", "bio15", "aridity_idx"))
set_desc <- c(A = "Stepwise-VIF set (no absolute temperature)", B = "Thermal extremes + seasonal moisture",
              C = "Mean temperature + annual moisture", D = "Thermal extremes + diurnal range",
              E = "Evaporative demand (VPD)", F = "Thermal extremes + annual moisture",
              G = "Mean temperature + seasonal moisture extremes", H = "Minimal (no diurnal range)",
              I = "Summer temperature", J = "Winter temperature")
cor_bg <- cor(bg_eval[, cand_vars], method = "spearman")
set_coll <- imap_dfr(cand_sets, function(v, nm) {
  cm <- abs(cor_bg[v, v]); diag(cm) <- 0
  tibble(set = nm, description = set_desc[nm], variables = paste(v, collapse = ", "),
         max_abs_rho = max(cm), max_VIF = max(usdm::vif(as.data.frame(bg_eval[, v]))$VIF))
})
```

## Model calibration, evaluation and selection

Models were fitted with MaxEnt 3.4 [@phillips2006; @phillips2017] through `dismo`, with clamping
enabled, threshold features disabled and complementary log-log (cloglog) output. Because the aim is
to predict suitability in a region where the species is invasive, models were evaluated primarily
on **transferability** [@wenger2012; @roberts2017], using two spatially structured
cross-validation schemes:

1. **Leave-one-region-out (LORO):** models were trained on two regions and tested on the third
   (East Asia, North America, Oceania). This is the most direct test of the task of interest,
   predicting suitability in a region from which no records were used.
2. **Spatial block cross-validation:** 5° × 5° blocks were randomly assigned to five folds, so
   training and test data were spatially separated within regions.

In each fold, training background points falling in the test region or blocks were withheld.
Test presences were contrasted with evaluation-background points from the same test region or
blocks. Discrimination within the test area was measured by the area under the ROC curve (AUC).
Calibration of the predicted presence/expected ratio was measured by the continuous Boyce index
(CBI) [@hirzel2006]. Over-fitting and transfer failure were measured by the omission rate of test
presences at the 10th-percentile training-presence threshold (OR10; expected value 0.10)
[@radosavljevic2014]. Configurations were selected with sequential criteria that prioritise
omission, following @radosavljevic2014 and @kass2021. First, we retained configurations with mean
LORO OR10 ≤ 0.30 and mean block OR10 ≤ 0.20. These bounds allow transferred models up to three times,
and within-region models up to twice, the expected omission of 0.10. Discrimination metrics alone
can be misleading under transfer: a model can rank sites correctly within a withheld region
(high AUC) while predicting uniformly low suitability there, and so omit almost all records at any
threshold calibrated on the training data. Second, the retained configurations were ranked on mean
AUC and CBI under each scheme, and the configuration with the lowest rank sum was selected.
The three top-ranked predictor sets were carried forward. For each, feature classes (L, LQ, LQH,
LQHP) and regularisation multipliers (β = 0.5–8) were tuned over the full grid with the same
criteria [@kass2021]. The top-ranked sets differed by small margins relative to the variation among
folds, so rather than relying on a single predictor set we combined the selected configuration of
each set into an unweighted consensus model (mean cloglog suitability of the three members). This
propagates uncertainty in predictor choice into the predictions. The consensus was evaluated with
exactly the same cross-validation folds, refitting all three members within each fold.

```{r}
#| label: cv-functions
#| code-summary: "Show code: model fitting and cross-validation functions"
fc_args <- function(fc) {
  f <- strsplit(fc, "")[[1]]
  c(paste0("linear=", "L" %in% f), paste0("quadratic=", "Q" %in% f), paste0("hinge=", "H" %in% f),
    paste0("product=", "P" %in% f), "threshold=false", "autofeature=false")
}
fit_mx <- function(p, a, vars, fc, rm) {
  x <- rbind(as.data.frame(p[, vars]), as.data.frame(a[, vars]))
  dismo::maxent(x = x, p = c(rep(1, nrow(p)), rep(0, nrow(a))),
                args = c(fc_args(fc), paste0("betamultiplier=", rm), "doclamp=true"))
}
pred_mx <- function(m, x, vars)
  as.numeric(dismo::predict(m, as.data.frame(x[, vars]), args = "outputformat=cloglog"))
auc_fun <- function(pp, pa) {             # Mann-Whitney AUC
  r <- rank(c(pp, pa)); np <- length(pp)
  (sum(r[seq_len(np)]) - np * (np + 1) / 2) / (np * length(pa)) }
cbi_fun <- function(pp, pa)
  tryCatch(ecospat.boyce(fit = c(pa, pp), obs = pp, nclass = 0, PEplot = FALSE)$cor, error = function(e) NA)

# Spatial blocks: 5-degree cells randomly allocated to 5 folds
blk_id <- function(lon, lat) paste(floor(lon / 5), floor(lat / 5))
set.seed(2024)
all_blk  <- unique(blk_id(c(occ$lon, bg_train$lon, bg_eval$lon, bg_uniform$lon),
                          c(occ$lat, bg_train$lat, bg_eval$lat, bg_uniform$lat)))
blk_fold <- setNames(sample(rep(1:5, length.out = length(all_blk))), all_blk)
add_block <- function(x) mutate(x, block = unname(blk_fold[blk_id(lon, lat)]))
occ <- add_block(occ); bg_train <- add_block(bg_train); bg_eval <- add_block(bg_eval)
bg_uniform <- add_block(bg_uniform)

run_cv <- function(vars, fc, rm, bg, scheme) {
  folds <- if (scheme == "loro") regs else 1:5
  ko <- if (scheme == "loro") occ$region else occ$block
  kb <- if (scheme == "loro") bg$region else bg$block
  ke <- if (scheme == "loro") bg_eval$region else bg_eval$block
  map_dfr(folds, function(k) {
    tr <- occ[ko != k, ]; te <- occ[ko == k, ]
    m  <- fit_mx(tr, bg[kb != k, ], vars, fc, rm)
    pp <- pred_mx(m, te, vars); pe <- pred_mx(m, bg_eval[ke == k, ], vars)
    thr <- quantile(pred_mx(m, tr, vars), 0.10)
    tibble(scheme = scheme, fold = as.character(k), n_test = nrow(te),
           auc = auc_fun(pp, pe), cbi = cbi_fun(pp, pe), or10 = mean(pp < thr))
  })
}
cv_summary <- function(cv) {
  l <- filter(cv, scheme == "loro"); b <- filter(cv, scheme == "block")
  tibble(loro_auc = mean(l$auc), loro_cbi = mean(l$cbi, na.rm = TRUE), loro_or10 = mean(l$or10),
         blk_auc = mean(b$auc), blk_cbi = mean(b$cbi, na.rm = TRUE), blk_or10 = mean(b$or10))
}
# Sequential selection: omission filter first, then rank sum of discrimination / calibration metrics
select_config <- function(d, max_or_loro = 0.30, max_or_blk = 0.20) {
  pass <- filter(d, loro_or10 <= max_or_loro, blk_or10 <= max_or_blk)
  if (nrow(pass) == 0) pass <- slice_min(d, loro_or10, n = 1)    # fallback: lowest transfer omission
  pass |> mutate(rank_sum = rank(-loro_auc) + rank(-loro_cbi) + rank(-blk_auc) + rank(-blk_cbi)) |>
    arrange(rank_sum)
}
# Consensus helpers: members = list of list(set, vars, fc, rm)
fit_ens  <- function(p, a, members) lapply(members, function(cf) fit_mx(p, a, cf$vars, cf$fc, cf$rm))
ens_pred_df <- function(ms, x) rowMeans(sapply(seq_along(ms), function(i) pred_mx(ms[[i]], x, members[[i]]$vars)))
ens_pred_rast <- function(ms, r) mean(rast(lapply(seq_along(ms), function(i)
  predict(r[[members[[i]]$vars]], ms[[i]], args = "outputformat=cloglog", na.rm = TRUE))))
run_cv_ens <- function(bg, scheme) {
  folds <- if (scheme == "loro") regs else 1:5
  ko <- if (scheme == "loro") occ$region else occ$block
  kb <- if (scheme == "loro") bg$region else bg$block
  ke <- if (scheme == "loro") bg_eval$region else bg_eval$block
  map_dfr(folds, function(k) {
    tr <- occ[ko != k, ]; te <- occ[ko == k, ]
    ms <- fit_ens(tr, bg[kb != k, ], members)
    pp <- ens_pred_df(ms, te); pe <- ens_pred_df(ms, bg_eval[ke == k, ])
    thr <- quantile(ens_pred_df(ms, tr), 0.10)
    tibble(scheme = scheme, fold = as.character(k), n_test = nrow(te),
           auc = auc_fun(pp, pe), cbi = cbi_fun(pp, pe), or10 = mean(pp < thr))
  })
}
run_grid <- function(grid, bg) {
  cl <- makeCluster(min(7, detectCores() - 1))
  on.exit(stopCluster(cl))
  clusterEvalQ(cl, { options(java.parameters = "-Xmx1g")
    suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(dismo); library(ecospat); library(dplyr); library(purrr); library(tibble) })
    NULL })
  clusterExport(cl, c("fc_args", "fit_mx", "pred_mx", "auc_fun", "cbi_fun", "run_cv", "cv_summary",
                      "occ", "bg_eval", "regs", "grid", "bg"), envir = environment())
  bind_rows(parLapplyLB(cl, seq_len(nrow(grid)), function(i) {
    g <- grid[i, ]; v <- g$vars[[1]]
    cv <- bind_rows(run_cv(v, g$fc, g$rm, bg, "loro"), run_cv(v, g$fc, g$rm, bg, "block"))
    bind_cols(dplyr::select(g, -vars), cv_summary(cv))
  }))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: select-variable-set
#| cache: true
# Stage 1: compare candidate variable sets across a reduced tuning grid
grid_sets <- expand_grid(set = names(cand_sets), fc = c("LQ", "LQH", "LQHP"), rm = c(1, 2, 4, 8)) |>
  mutate(vars = cand_sets[set])
set_res <- run_grid(grid_sets, bg_train) |> mutate(pass = loro_or10 <= 0.30 & blk_or10 <= 0.20)
ranked_sets <- select_config(set_res)
sel_sets <- head(unique(ranked_sets$set), 3)     # three top-ranked predictor sets
# Best configuration per set: best-ranked passing configuration, or (if none pass) lowest transfer omission
best_by_set <- bind_rows(
  ranked_sets |> group_by(set) |> slice_min(rank_sum, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE),
  set_res |> filter(!set %in% ranked_sets$set) |> group_by(set) |> slice_min(loro_or10, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)) |>
  ungroup() |> arrange(!pass, rank_sum, loro_or10)
# Per-region transfer of the temperature-free set A in its best-discriminating configuration
a_best <- set_res |> filter(set == "A") |>
  mutate(r = rank(-loro_auc) + rank(-loro_cbi) + rank(-blk_auc) + rank(-blk_cbi)) |> slice_min(r, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
cv_A <- run_cv(cand_sets$A, a_best$fc, a_best$rm, bg_train, "loro")
write_csv(set_res, file.path(out_dir, "candidate_set_cv_grid.csv"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tune-model
#| cache: true
# Stage 2: full tuning grid for each of the three top-ranked predictor sets
grid_tune <- expand_grid(set = sel_sets, fc = c("L", "LQ", "LQH", "LQHP"), rm = c(0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8)) |>
  mutate(vars = cand_sets[set])
tune_all <- run_grid(grid_tune, bg_train)
tune_sel <- map_dfr(sel_sets, ~ select_config(filter(tune_all, set == .x)) |> slice(1))
members  <- pmap(tune_sel |> dplyr::select(set, fc, rm), function(set, fc, rm)
  list(set = set, vars = cand_sets[[set]], fc = fc, rm = rm))
names(members) <- sel_sets
sel_vars <- unique(unlist(map(members, "vars")))          # union of predictors used by the consensus
sel_vars <- cand_vars[cand_vars %in% sel_vars]
write_csv(tune_all, file.path(out_dir, "tuning_cv_grid.csv"))
```

Each consensus member was refitted to all records. Variable importance was summarised as MaxEnt
permutation importance of each member [@phillips2017]. Marginal response curves of the consensus
were computed with the other predictors held at their median value across presence records.
Uncertainty was quantified by refitting the model to 30 bootstrap resamples of the presence records
(resampling within regions to preserve regional composition; all three members were refitted to each
resample). We report the across-replicate 95%
interval for response curves and the across-replicate standard deviation for mapped suitability.

```{r}
#| label: final-model
#| cache: true
m_final <- fit_ens(occ, bg_train, members)          # list of the three member models
saveRDS(list(members = members, models = m_final), file.path(proc_v3, "final_consensus_models.rds"))

var_imp <- imap_dfr(m_final, function(m, nm) {
  v <- members[[nm]]$vars; r <- m@results
  tibble(set = nm, variable = v, contribution = r[paste0(v, ".contribution"), 1],
         permutation = r[paste0(v, ".permutation.importance"), 1]) })
imp_order <- var_imp |> group_by(variable) |> summarise(mean_perm = sum(permutation) / length(members)) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_perm))
n_feat <- map_int(m_final, function(m) {
  lam <- m@lambdas; lam <- lam[!grepl("^(linearPredictorNormalizer|densityNormalizer|numBackgroundPoints|entropy)", lam)]
  sum(as.numeric(sapply(strsplit(lam, ","), `[`, 2)) != 0) })

# Consensus cross-validation by fold (all members refitted within each fold)
cv_final <- bind_rows(run_cv_ens(bg_train, "loro"), run_cv_ens(bg_train, "block"))
cvs_final <- cv_summary(cv_final)
write_csv(cv_final, file.path(out_dir, "final_model_cv_folds.csv"))

# Thresholds and in-sample discrimination
p_occ  <- ens_pred_df(m_final, occ)
p_eval <- ens_pred_df(m_final, bg_eval)
thr_p10 <- unname(quantile(p_occ, 0.10))
ev <- dismo::evaluate(p = p_occ, a = p_eval)
thr_mss <- ev@t[which.max(ev@TPR + ev@TNR)]
insample <- tibble(region = regs) |>
  mutate(auc = map_dbl(region, ~ auc_fun(p_occ[occ$region == .x], p_eval[bg_eval$region == .x])),
         cbi = map_dbl(region, ~ cbi_fun(p_occ[occ$region == .x], p_eval[bg_eval$region == .x])),
         pct_suitable = map_dbl(region, ~ 100 * mean(p_occ[occ$region == .x] >= thr_p10)))
auc_all <- auc_fun(p_occ, p_eval); cbi_all <- cbi_fun(p_occ, p_eval)
```

```{r}
#| label: bootstrap
#| cache: true
n_boot <- 30
set.seed(31)
boot_models <- map(seq_len(n_boot), function(b) {
  idx <- unlist(lapply(regs, function(r) { i <- which(occ$region == r); i[sample.int(length(i), replace = TRUE)] }))
  fit_ens(occ[idx, ], bg_train, members)
})
```

## Projection to Australia and New Zealand

The consensus model was projected onto Australia and New Zealand (110–180°E, 8–48°S, restricted to the
land area of the two countries). Climatic suitability was converted to suitable/unsuitable using the
10th-percentile training-presence threshold. This threshold is appropriate for presence-background
data and tolerates a small proportion of erroneous or sink-population records [@liu2013]; the
threshold maximising sensitivity + specificity against the evaluation background is reported for
comparison. Extrapolation was assessed with the multivariate environmental similarity surface (MESS)
and the most dissimilar variable [@elith2010], using presence and training-background environments
as the reference. To identify the climatic factor constraining suitability in each grid cell, we
computed limiting factors following @elith2010: for each predictor in turn, its value was set to the
median across presence records and the predictor yielding the largest increase in suitability was
taken as limiting.

To identify candidate areas for surveillance, suitable cells were classified by their geodesic
distance to the nearest known Oceanian record (training records plus all georeferenced ALA records).
Suitable cells more than 100 km from any known record were designated as *suitable but unrecorded*.
Areas were computed from true (latitude-dependent) cell areas and summarised by Australian
state/territory and New Zealand island.

```{r}
#| label: projection
aunz_poly <- world10 |> filter(admin %in% c("Australia", "New Zealand")) |> st_union() |> vect()
env_au <- crop(env_all[[sel_vars]], ext(110, 180, -48, -8)) |> mask(aunz_poly)
pred_cur <- ens_pred_rast(m_final, env_au)
names(pred_cur) <- "suitability"
writeRaster(pred_cur, file.path(proc_v3, "suitability_current_aunz.tif"), overwrite = TRUE)

# Bootstrap prediction uncertainty
boot_stack <- rast(lapply(boot_models, ens_pred_rast, r = env_au))
boot_sd   <- app(boot_stack, sd)
boot_bin  <- app(boot_stack >= thr_p10, mean)          # proportion of replicates predicting suitable
names(boot_sd) <- "sd"; names(boot_bin) <- "agreement"
writeRaster(boot_sd, file.path(proc_v3, "suitability_bootstrap_sd_aunz.tif"), overwrite = TRUE)

# Extrapolation (MESS) relative to calibration environments
ref_env <- bind_rows(occ[, sel_vars], bg_train[, sel_vars])
mess_full <- predicts::mess(env_au, as.data.frame(ref_env), full = TRUE)
mess_r <- mess_full[["mess"]]
mod_r  <- which.min(mess_full[[paste0(sel_vars, "_mess")]]); mod_r <- mask(mod_r, mess_r < 0, maskvalues = 0)
writeRaster(mess_r, file.path(proc_v3, "mess_current_aunz.tif"), overwrite = TRUE)

# Limiting factors (Elith et al. 2010)
gain <- rast(lapply(sel_vars, function(v) {
  e2 <- env_au; e2[[v]] <- mask(init(e2[[v]], median(occ[[v]])), e2[[v]])
  ens_pred_rast(m_final, e2) - pred_cur }))
names(gain) <- sel_vars
limit_r <- which.max(gain)

# Binary suitability and surveillance gaps
suit_bin <- pred_cur >= thr_p10
ala <- read_csv(file.path(base_dir, "data", "ALA_occurence", "records-2026-02-04.csv"),
                show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  transmute(lon = decimalLongitude, lat = decimalLatitude) |> drop_na()
known <- bind_rows(occ |> filter(region == "Oceania") |> dplyr::select(lon, lat), ala) |> distinct()
dist_known <- distance(pred_cur, vect(known, geom = c("lon", "lat"), crs = "EPSG:4326")) / 1000
dist_known <- mask(dist_known, pred_cur)
gap_r <- ifel(suit_bin == 0, 0, ifel(dist_known <= 100, 1, 2))   # 0 unsuitable, 1 suitable near records, 2 gap

# Jurisdictions (Australian states/territories; NZ islands)
jur <- ne_states(country = c("Australia", "New Zealand"), returnclass = "sf") |>
  mutate(jur = case_when(admin == "Australia" & name %in% c("Jervis Bay Territory", "Lord Howe Island", "Macquarie Island") ~ "Other territories",
                         admin == "Australia" ~ name,
                         region == "North Island" ~ "NZ North Island",
                         region == "South Island" ~ "NZ South Island",
                         TRUE ~ "NZ outlying islands")) |>
  group_by(jur) |> summarise(geometry = st_union(geometry), .groups = "drop")
jur_r  <- rasterize(vect(jur), pred_cur, field = "jur")
carea  <- cellSize(pred_cur, unit = "km") |> mask(pred_cur)
zone_area <- function(x) { z <- zonal(carea * x, jur_r, fun = "sum", na.rm = TRUE); setNames(z[[2]], z[[1]]) }
area_tab <- tibble(jurisdiction = levels(jur_r)[[1]]$jur) |>
  mutate(land_km2     = zone_area(carea > 0)[jurisdiction],
         suitable_km2 = zone_area(suit_bin)[jurisdiction],
         suitable_analog_km2 = zone_area(suit_bin * (mess_r >= 0))[jurisdiction],
         gap_km2      = zone_area(gap_r == 2)[jurisdiction]) |>
  filter(land_km2 > 1000) |>
  mutate(pct_suitable = 100 * suitable_km2 / land_km2) |> arrange(desc(suitable_km2))
write_csv(area_tab, file.path(out_dir, "suitable_area_by_jurisdiction.csv"))
tot <- global(c(carea, carea * suit_bin, carea * (mess_r < 0), carea * (gap_r == 2)), "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]
names(tot) <- c("land", "suitable", "novel", "gap")
```

## Niche comparison between native and invaded ranges

To understand why transfer between regions succeeds or fails, we compared the realised climatic niche
of the native range (East Asia) with each invaded range in a common environmental space
[@broennimann2012; @dicola2017]. A principal component analysis (PCA) of the selected predictors
was calibrated on the evaluation background across all three regions. Occurrence and background
densities were estimated on a 100 × 100 grid of the first two axes. We calculated Schoener's *D*,
niche equivalency and similarity tests (100 randomisations; similarity with the native niche held
fixed) [@warren2008], and the niche dynamics indices of stability, expansion and unfilling
calculated in climates shared by both ranges (intersection = 0.1) [@guisan2014].

```{r}
#| label: niche
#| cache: true
pca <- dudi.pca(bg_eval[, sel_vars], scannf = FALSE, nf = 2)
sc_bg  <- pca$li
sc_occ <- suprow(pca, occ[, sel_vars])$li
grid_z <- function(r) ecospat.grid.clim.dyn(glob = sc_bg, glob1 = sc_bg[bg_eval$region == r, ],
                                          sp = sc_occ[occ$region == r, ], R = 100, th.sp = 0, th.env = 0)
z <- setNames(lapply(regs, grid_z), regs)
niche_cmp <- function(nat, inv) {
  set.seed(7)
  eq  <- ecospat.niche.equivalency.test(z[[nat]], z[[inv]], rep = 100, overlap.alternative = "lower", ncores = 1)
  sim <- ecospat.niche.similarity.test(z[[nat]], z[[inv]], rep = 100, rand.type = 2, ncores = 1)
  dyn <- ecospat.niche.dyn.index(z[[nat]], z[[inv]], intersection = 0.1)$dynamic.index.w
  list(eq = eq, sim = sim,
       tab = tibble(comparison = paste(reg_lab[nat], "vs", reg_lab[inv]),
                    D = ecospat.niche.overlap(z[[nat]], z[[inv]], cor = TRUE)$D,
                    p_equivalency = eq$p.D, p_similarity = sim$p.D,
                    stability = dyn[["stability"]], expansion = dyn[["expansion"]], unfilling = dyn[["unfilling"]]))
}
nc_oc <- niche_cmp("East_Asia", "Oceania")
nc_na <- niche_cmp("East_Asia", "North_America")
niche_tab <- bind_rows(nc_oc$tab, nc_na$tab)
write_csv(niche_tab, file.path(out_dir, "niche_comparison.csv"))
```

## Sensitivity analysis

To test whether conclusions depended on the sampling-bias correction, the consensus members were
refitted with a background drawn uniformly across *M* (same regional allocation, no target-group
weighting), and its cross-validated performance and Australian/New Zealand predictions were compared
with those of the final model.

```{r}
#| label: sensitivity
m_unif <- fit_ens(occ, bg_uniform, members)
cv_unif <- bind_rows(run_cv_ens(bg_uniform, "loro"), run_cv_ens(bg_uniform, "block"))
pred_unif <- ens_pred_rast(m_unif, env_au)
thr_unif  <- quantile(ens_pred_df(m_unif, occ), 0.10)
sens_vals <- na.omit(cbind(values(pred_cur), values(pred_unif)))
sens_cor  <- cor(sens_vals[, 1], sens_vals[, 2], method = "spearman")
bin_agree <- mean((sens_vals[, 1] >= thr_p10) == (sens_vals[, 2] >= thr_unif))
```

All analyses were run in R `r paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = ".")` using `terra`,
`sf`, `dismo` `r packageVersion("dismo")` (bundled MaxEnt 3.4 Java executable), `predicts`, `ecospat` and the `tidyverse`.

# Results

## Occurrence data and calibration environments

The final dataset comprised `r n_occ` thinned records: `r n_by_reg[["East_Asia"]]` from the native
East Asian range, `r n_by_reg[["North_America"]]` from North America and `r n_by_reg[["Oceania"]]`
from Oceania (@fig-occ; @supptbl-occ). The accessible area covered
`r fmt_int(sum(reg_area)/1e6)` million km² of land, of which East Asia, North America and Oceania
made up `r fmt(100*reg_share[1],0)`%, `r fmt(100*reg_share[2],0)`% and `r fmt(100*reg_share[3],0)`%,
respectively. The `r fmt_int(nrow(tg))` de-duplicated target-group tick records were
strongly concentrated in North America (`r fmt(100*mean(tg$region=="North_America"),0)`%),
confirming the need for region-specific normalisation of the sampling-effort surface
(@suppfig-bias). Presence records occupied a subset of the available environments in each region,
generally the warmer, wetter and less arid portion of *M* (@suppfig-envdens).

::: {.primary-figure}
```{r}
#| label: fig-occ
#| fig-cap: "Occurrence records of *Haemaphysalis longicornis* used for model calibration (n = 389 after 10-km thinning and regional stratification), coloured by calibration region. Shading shows the accessible area (*M*; union of 1,000-km buffers around records, clipped to land). (a) Global view; (b) Australia, New Zealand and the south-west Pacific."
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 8.5
world50 <- ne_countries(scale = 50, returnclass = "sf")
M_df <- as.data.frame(aggregate(M_r, 4, fun = "max", na.rm = TRUE), xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)
p_glob <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = world50, fill = "grey93", colour = "grey75", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_tile(data = M_df, aes(x, y), fill = "#9ecae1", alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_point(data = occ, aes(lon, lat, colour = region), size = 1.1, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = reg_col, labels = reg_lab, name = NULL) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-180, 180), ylim = c(-55, 75), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, tag = "a") + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
p_oce <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = world50, fill = "grey93", colour = "grey75", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_tile(data = filter(M_df, x > 105, y < -5), aes(x, y), fill = "#9ecae1", alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_point(data = filter(occ, region == "Oceania"), aes(lon, lat), colour = reg_col["Oceania"], size = 1.4) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(110, 180), ylim = c(-48, -10), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, tag = "b")
p_fig1 <- p_glob / p_oce + plot_layout(heights = c(1.1, 1))
p_fig1
save_fig("Fig1_occurrences_M", p_fig1, 11, 8.5)
```
:::

## Variable selection and model tuning

Of the `r nrow(set_res)` set × configuration combinations, `r nrow(ranked_sets)` passed the omission
filter, all of them from sets `r paste(sort(unique(ranked_sets$set)), collapse = ", ")`
(@supptbl-sets). Every one of these sets includes a direct temperature variable. The
temperature-free set A had no passing configuration. In its best-discriminating configuration
(`r a_best$fc`, β = `r a_best$rm`), set A ranked sites well within the withheld regions (mean LORO
AUC = `r fmt(a_best$loro_auc)`) but failed to transfer suitability levels: when Oceania was withheld,
`r fmt(100*filter(cv_A, fold == "Oceania")$or10, 0)`% of Oceanian records fell below the training
threshold (East Asia: `r fmt(100*filter(cv_A, fold == "East_Asia")$or10, 0)`%). The three top-ranked
sets were `r paste(sel_sets, collapse = ", ")`. All of them combine annual mean temperature with
moisture-supply and aridity variables, and they differed only marginally in performance
(@supptbl-sets). After tuning, the consensus members were
`r paste(map_chr(members, ~ sprintf("set %s (%s; %s, β = %s; %d features)", .x$set, paste(.x$vars, collapse = ", "), .x$fc, .x$rm, n_feat[[.x$set]])), collapse = "; ")`.
Simple, regularised configurations transferred best in all three sets (@suppfig-tuning).

## Model performance

The consensus model discriminated presences from available environments in every withheld region
(@tbl-perf; @supptbl-folds). Transfer to Oceania from the native and North American records alone
was strong (AUC = `r fmt(filter(cv_final, fold=="Oceania")$auc)`,
CBI = `r fmt(filter(cv_final, fold=="Oceania")$cbi)`), indicating that the climatic conditions
occupied in Australia and New Zealand are predictable from the rest of the range. Transfer to East
Asia was the weakest (AUC = `r fmt(filter(cv_final, fold=="East_Asia")$auc)`) and had the highest
omission (OR10 = `r fmt(filter(cv_final, fold=="East_Asia")$or10)`): models trained only on the
invaded ranges under-predict the colder and more continental parts of the native range. Spatial
block cross-validation gave mean AUC = `r fmt(cvs_final$blk_auc)`,
CBI = `r fmt(cvs_final$blk_cbi)` and OR10 = `r fmt(cvs_final$blk_or10)`, moderately above the
expected 0.10. Applied to the full dataset, the model classified
`r fmt(filter(insample, region=="Oceania")$pct_suitable, 0)`% of Oceanian,
`r fmt(filter(insample, region=="North_America")$pct_suitable, 0)`% of North American and
`r fmt(filter(insample, region=="East_Asia")$pct_suitable, 0)`% of East Asian records as suitable at
the 10th-percentile threshold (cloglog = `r fmt(thr_p10, 3)`; @supptbl-thr).

::: {.primary-table}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-perf
#| tbl-cap: "Evaluation of the consensus MaxEnt model. Cross-validated metrics are computed on withheld records against evaluation-background points from the same withheld region or blocks. AUC = area under the ROC curve; CBI = continuous Boyce index; OR10 = omission rate at the 10th-percentile training-presence threshold (expected 0.10). In-sample metrics use the consensus fitted to all records against the evaluation background of each region."
perf_tab <- bind_rows(
  cv_final |> filter(scheme == "loro") |>
    transmute(Evaluation = "Leave-one-region-out", `Test data` = reg_lab[fold], n = n_test, AUC = auc, CBI = cbi, OR10 = or10),
  cv_final |> filter(scheme == "block") |>
    summarise(Evaluation = "Spatial block CV (5 folds)", `Test data` = "Mean across folds", n = sum(n_test),
              AUC = mean(auc), CBI = mean(cbi, na.rm = TRUE), OR10 = mean(or10)),
  insample |> transmute(Evaluation = "In-sample (full model)", `Test data` = reg_lab[region],
                        n = as.integer(n_by_reg[region]), AUC = auc, CBI = cbi, OR10 = 1 - pct_suitable / 100))
write_csv(perf_tab, file.path(out_dir, "model_performance.csv"))
kable(perf_tab, digits = 3)
```
:::

## Variable importance and response curves

Annual mean temperature was the only predictor that was important in all three consensus members
(permutation importance `r fmt(min(filter(var_imp, variable == "bio1")$permutation), 0)`–`r fmt(max(filter(var_imp, variable == "bio1")$permutation), 0)`%).
The aridity index (sets H and C) and mean diurnal temperature range (sets C and G) carried most of
the remaining importance (@fig-response a). Precipitation amounts were largely redundant once aridity
and temperature were included. Annual precipitation and wettest-month precipitation were regularised
to near-zero importance, and their marginal responses were flat. Consensus suitability was unimodal
in annual mean temperature, peaking at about 12–15 °C and falling steeply below about 5 °C and above
about 20 °C. It declined monotonically with increasing aridity and with increasing diurnal
temperature range, the latter characterising continental and inland climates (@fig-response b).
Suitability rose weakly at high precipitation seasonality. This reflects the monsoonal summer-rainfall
climates of the core native range in eastern China, and the bootstrap interval is wide there.

::: {.primary-figure}
```{r}
#| label: fig-response
#| fig-cap: "Predictor importance and responses in the consensus model. (a) Permutation importance of each predictor in each consensus member (predictors absent from a member have no bar). (b) Marginal response curves of the consensus (mean cloglog suitability of the three members), with other predictors held at their median across presences; the line is the fitted consensus and the ribbon the 95% interval across 30 bootstrap replicates. Rugs show the predictor values at presence records, coloured by region."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 9
lvl <- var_lab[imp_order$variable]
p_imp <- var_imp |> mutate(variable = factor(var_lab[variable], levels = rev(lvl)), set = paste("Set", set)) |>
  ggplot(aes(permutation, variable, fill = set)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge2(preserve = "single", width = 0.8), width = 0.75) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = "Consensus member") +
  labs(x = "Permutation importance (%)", y = NULL, tag = "a") + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

med <- occ |> summarise(across(all_of(sel_vars), median))
resp_grid <- map_dfr(sel_vars, function(v) {
  rng <- quantile(c(occ[[v]], bg_train[[v]]), c(0.005, 0.995))
  nd <- med[rep(1, 200), ]; nd[[v]] <- seq(rng[1], rng[2], length.out = 200)
  boot <- sapply(boot_models, ens_pred_df, x = nd)
  tibble(variable = v, x = nd[[v]], fit = ens_pred_df(m_final, nd),
         lo = apply(boot, 1, quantile, 0.025), hi = apply(boot, 1, quantile, 0.975))
}) |> mutate(variable = factor(var_lab[variable], levels = lvl))
rug_df <- occ |> dplyr::select(region, all_of(sel_vars)) |> pivot_longer(-region, names_to = "variable", values_to = "x") |>
  mutate(variable = factor(var_lab[variable], levels = lvl))
p_resp <- ggplot(resp_grid, aes(x)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#2c7fb8", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit), colour = "#08519c", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_rug(data = rug_df, aes(x = x, colour = region), sides = "b", alpha = 0.5, length = unit(0.04, "npc")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = reg_col, labels = reg_lab, name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_x", ncol = 3) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Consensus suitability (cloglog)", tag = "b") + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
p_fig2 <- p_imp + p_resp + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 2.3))
p_fig2
save_fig("Fig2_importance_response", p_fig2, 12, 9)
```
:::

## Current climatic suitability of Australia and New Zealand

Suitable climate for *H. longicornis* is concentrated along the eastern seaboard of Australia, from
south-east Queensland through coastal New South Wales and eastern and southern Victoria, and across
Tasmania. Smaller areas lie in south-western Western Australia and the south-east of South
Australia. Most of New Zealand is suitable (@fig-suit). In total, `r fmt_int(tot[["suitable"]])` km²
(`r fmt(100*tot[["suitable"]]/tot[["land"]],1)`% of the two countries' land area) was classified as
suitable (@tbl-area). Only `r fmt(100*tot[["novel"]]/tot[["land"]],1)`% of the land area had climates
outside the calibration range (MESS < 0), almost entirely in the tropical north-west of Australia,
where suitability is negligible (@suppfig-mess). Bootstrap uncertainty was low across most of the
two countries. It was highest along the margins of the suitable area, notably inland Victoria,
south-western Western Australia and the eastern South Island. More than 95% of replicates agreed on
the binary classification of the core eastern Australian, Tasmanian and New Zealand ranges
(@suppfig-boot). Victoria (`r fmt(filter(area_tab, jurisdiction == "Victoria")$pct_suitable, 0)`%),
New South Wales (`r fmt(filter(area_tab, jurisdiction == "New South Wales")$pct_suitable, 0)`%) and
Tasmania (`r fmt(filter(area_tab, jurisdiction == "Tasmania")$pct_suitable, 0)`%) had the largest
suitable proportions in Australia. Queensland's large total land area translated into only
`r fmt_int(filter(area_tab, jurisdiction == "Queensland")$suitable_km2)` km² of suitable climate,
confined to the south-east and a few coastal and upland pockets further north. The Northern
Territory had none. The global projection reproduced the native distribution in eastern China, the
Korean Peninsula and Japan and the invaded range in the eastern United States (@suppfig-global).

::: {.primary-figure}
```{r}
#| label: fig-suit
#| fig-cap: "Current climatic suitability for *Haemaphysalis longicornis* in Australia and New Zealand. (a) Continuous cloglog suitability with known Oceanian records (training records and ALA records; black points). (b) Binary suitability at the 10th-percentile training-presence threshold; pale colours indicate cells with climates outside the calibration range (MESS < 0)."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6
aunz_sf <- world10 |> filter(admin %in% c("Australia", "New Zealand"))
bin_cls <- (suit_bin + 1) + 2 * (mess_r < 0)       # 1 unsuitable, 2 suitable, 3 unsuitable-novel, 4 suitable-novel
bin_cls <- as.factor(bin_cls)
levels(bin_cls) <- data.frame(ID = 1:4, class = c("Unsuitable", "Suitable", "Unsuitable (novel climate)", "Suitable (novel climate)"))
map_base <- list(coord_sf(xlim = c(112, 179), ylim = c(-47.5, -10), expand = FALSE),
                 labs(x = NULL, y = NULL), theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#f4f8fb", colour = NA)))
p_cont <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = pred_cur, maxcell = 2e6) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, limits = c(0, 1), na.value = NA, name = "Suitability") +
  geom_sf(data = aunz_sf, fill = NA, colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_point(data = known, aes(lon, lat), size = 0.6, colour = "black") +
  map_base + labs(tag = "a")
p_bin <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = bin_cls, maxcell = 2e6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Unsuitable" = "grey88", "Suitable" = "#2166ac",
                               "Unsuitable (novel climate)" = "#f6e8c3", "Suitable (novel climate)" = "#92c5de"),
                    na.value = NA, na.translate = FALSE, name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  geom_sf(data = aunz_sf, fill = NA, colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.15) +
  map_base + labs(tag = "b") + theme(legend.position = "bottom") + guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
p_fig3 <- p_cont + p_bin
p_fig3
save_fig("Fig3_current_suitability", p_fig3, 12, 6)
```

```{r}
area_print <- area_tab |>
  transmute(Jurisdiction = jurisdiction, `Land (km²)` = fmt_int(land_km2), `Suitable (km²)` = fmt_int(suitable_km2),
            `Suitable (%)` = fmt(pct_suitable, 1), `Suitable, analogue (km²)` = fmt_int(suitable_analog_km2),
            `Suitable but unrecorded (km²)` = fmt_int(gap_km2))
kable(area_print, align = "lrrrrr")
```

## Niche comparison between native and invaded ranges

In the climatic space defined by the model predictors (first two PCA axes explaining
`r fmt(100*sum(pca$eig[1:2])/sum(pca$eig), 0)`% of the variation), the Oceanian and native niches
overlapped moderately (Schoener's *D* = `r fmt(nc_oc$tab$D)`). Niche equivalency could not be
rejected (P = `r fmt(nc_oc$tab$p_equivalency)`), and the Oceanian niche was more similar to the
native niche than expected from the climates available in Oceania (P = `r fmt(nc_oc$tab$p_similarity, 3)`;
@supptbl-niche, @suppfig-nichetests). Within climates shared by both ranges, `r fmt(100*nc_oc$tab$stability, 0)`%
of the Oceanian niche coincided with the native niche (stability). Expansion into climates unused in
the native range was limited (`r fmt(100*nc_oc$tab$expansion, 0)`%). It was directed towards wet
climates with evenly distributed rainfall and substantial dry-season precipitation (high PC2; low
BIO15, high BIO17), typical of New Zealand and coastal south-eastern Australia (@fig-niche a). About
a third of the native niche was unfilled in Oceania (`r fmt(100*nc_oc$tab$unfilling, 0)`%). This
part corresponds to drier, strongly seasonal summer-rainfall climates with dry winters and larger
diurnal temperature ranges (high PC1, low PC2), characteristic of northern and inland China. In contrast, the North American niche overlapped very little with the native niche
(*D* = `r fmt(nc_na$tab$D)`) and was not equivalent to it (P = `r fmt(nc_na$tab$p_equivalency, 3)`).
This was not because of expansion into novel climates. Rather, North American records occupy a small
part of the climates available there, leaving `r fmt(100*nc_na$tab$unfilling, 0)`% of the native
niche unfilled (@fig-niche b).

::: {.primary-figure}
```{r}
#| label: fig-niche
#| fig-cap: "Niche dynamics of *H. longicornis* in climatic space (first two PCA axes of the model predictors, calibrated on the background of all regions). Blue = niche stability (climates occupied in both ranges); red = expansion (occupied only in the invaded range); green = unfilling (occupied only in the native range); colour intensity reflects occurrence density. Green and red contours delimit the climates available in the native and invaded ranges, respectively (100%, and 75% for the paler line). Arrows show the shift from the native to the invaded niche centroid (solid) and background centroid (dashed). (a) East Asia vs. Oceania; (b) East Asia vs. North America."
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5.5
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for (inv in c("Oceania", "North_America")) {
  ecospat.plot.niche.dyn(z[["East_Asia"]], z[[inv]], quant = 0.25, interest = 2,
                         title = paste(ifelse(inv == "Oceania", "(a)", "(b)"), "East Asia vs.", gsub("_", " ", inv)),
                         name.axis1 = sprintf("PC1 (%.0f%%)", 100 * pca$eig[1] / sum(pca$eig)),
                         name.axis2 = sprintf("PC2 (%.0f%%)", 100 * pca$eig[2] / sum(pca$eig)))
  ecospat.shift.centroids(sc_occ[occ$region == "East_Asia", ], sc_occ[occ$region == inv, ],
                          sc_bg[bg_eval$region == "East_Asia", ], sc_bg[bg_eval$region == inv, ])
}
png(file.path(fig_dir, "Fig4_niche_dynamics.png"), width = 11, height = 5.5, units = "in", res = 300)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for (inv in c("Oceania", "North_America")) {
  ecospat.plot.niche.dyn(z[["East_Asia"]], z[[inv]], quant = 0.25, interest = 2,
                         title = paste(ifelse(inv == "Oceania", "(a)", "(b)"), "East Asia vs.", gsub("_", " ", inv)),
                         name.axis1 = "PC1", name.axis2 = "PC2")
  ecospat.shift.centroids(sc_occ[occ$region == "East_Asia", ], sc_occ[occ$region == inv, ],
                          sc_bg[bg_eval$region == "East_Asia", ], sc_bg[bg_eval$region == inv, ])
}
invisible(dev.off())
```
:::

## Limiting factors and surveillance gaps

Aridity was the most limiting factor across most of inland Australia. Mean diurnal temperature
range was limiting along the western slopes and tablelands of the Great Dividing Range, immediately
inland of the suitable eastern belt. High annual mean temperature was limiting across the tropical
north (@fig-limit a). In Tasmania, the South Island and upland areas of New Zealand, low annual mean
temperature was the main factor reducing suitability below its optimum, although most of these areas
still exceeded the suitability threshold. Of the suitable area, `r fmt_int(tot[["gap"]])` km²
(`r fmt(100*tot[["gap"]]/tot[["suitable"]], 0)`%) lay more than 100 km from any known Oceanian record
(@fig-limit b; @tbl-area). Most of this was in the NZ South Island
(`r fmt_int(filter(area_tab, jurisdiction == "NZ South Island")$gap_km2)` km²), Tasmania
(`r fmt_int(filter(area_tab, jurisdiction == "Tasmania")$gap_km2)` km²), western and coastal Victoria
(`r fmt_int(filter(area_tab, jurisdiction == "Victoria")$gap_km2)` km²), coastal Queensland north of
the main known range (`r fmt_int(filter(area_tab, jurisdiction == "Queensland")$gap_km2)` km²) and the
south-east of South Australia (`r fmt_int(filter(area_tab, jurisdiction == "South Australia")$gap_km2)` km²).

::: {.primary-figure}
```{r}
#| label: fig-limit
#| fig-cap: "(a) Most limiting climatic factor in each grid cell (the predictor whose adjustment to its median value at presence records would most increase suitability; Elith et al. 2010). (b) Suitable climate relative to known records: suitable cells within 100 km of a known Oceanian record, and suitable cells more than 100 km from any known record (candidate surveillance areas)."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6
lim_f <- as.factor(limit_r)
levels(lim_f) <- data.frame(ID = seq_along(sel_vars), factor = var_lab[sel_vars])
lim_cols <- setNames(c("#e41a1c", "#ff7f00", "#4daf4a", "#377eb8", "#984ea3", "#a65628", "#f781bf", "#999999")[seq_along(sel_vars)], var_lab[sel_vars])
p_lim <- ggplot() + geom_spatraster(data = lim_f, maxcell = 2e6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = lim_cols, na.value = NA, na.translate = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  geom_sf(data = aunz_sf, fill = NA, colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.15) +
  map_base + labs(tag = "a") + theme(legend.position = "bottom") + guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
gap_f <- as.factor(gap_r)
levels(gap_f) <- data.frame(ID = 0:2, class = c("Unsuitable", "Suitable, ≤100 km from known record", "Suitable, >100 km from known records"))
p_gap <- ggplot() + geom_spatraster(data = gap_f, maxcell = 2e6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey88", "#4393c3", "#d6604d"), na.value = NA, na.translate = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  geom_sf(data = aunz_sf, fill = NA, colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_point(data = known, aes(lon, lat), size = 0.5, colour = "black") +
  map_base + labs(tag = "b") + theme(legend.position = "bottom") + guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
p_fig5 <- p_lim + p_gap
p_fig5
save_fig("Fig5_limiting_factors_gaps", p_fig5, 12, 6)
```
:::

# Discussion

We developed a consensus species distribution model for *H. longicornis* that was selected for, and
demonstrably capable of, transfer between continents. Trained without any Oceanian records, it
reproduced the known Australian and New Zealand distribution, ranking occupied sites far above
available environments (AUC = `r fmt(filter(cv_final, fold == "Oceania")$auc)`; Boyce index =
`r fmt(filter(cv_final, fold == "Oceania")$cbi)`). Fitted to all records, the model indicates that
current climate permits *H. longicornis* across `r fmt_int(tot[["suitable"]])` km² of Australia and
New Zealand. This area is concentrated on the humid, thermally equable eastern seaboard of Australia,
Tasmania and almost all of New Zealand, and is bounded inland by aridity and continental temperature
regimes and to the north by heat.

## Transferability depends on predictors and sampling design

Two methodological choices largely determined whether the model transferred. The first was the
treatment of sampling bias. GBIF tick records, the usual source of target-group background, are
dominated by North American data. A single global sampling-effort surface would therefore place most
background points in North America and contrast East Asian and Oceanian presences against very few
local background points. Normalising sampling effort within regions and allocating background in
proportion to area keeps the correction for survey intensity within regions without letting
differences in data volume among countries dominate the fitted niche. Predictions were nearly
identical with a uniform background (Spearman ρ = `r fmt(sens_cor)`; @suppfig-sens), so the
conclusions do not depend on the details of the bias surface.

The second was the predictor set. Automated stepwise VIF selection removed every absolute
temperature variable because temperature is strongly collinear with VPD, PET and the thermal
extremes. The resulting predictor set (set A) discriminated well within withheld regions but failed
to transfer suitability levels: with Oceania withheld, `r fmt(100*filter(cv_A, fold == "Oceania")$or10, 0)`%
of Oceanian records fell below the training threshold. Correlated variables such as VPD and
isothermality can stand in for temperature within a calibration region, but the relationships among
them differ between continents. Only a direct thermal gradient constrains predictions consistently.
This is biologically expected. Development rates, questing activity and overwinter survival of ixodid
ticks are governed by temperature, and off-host survival is governed by the atmospheric moisture
balance [@needham1991; @heath2016]. The three predictor sets retained in the consensus each pair
annual mean temperature with a moisture or desiccation axis, which matches this mechanistic
expectation. Our results add to evidence that selecting predictors on ecological grounds and
evaluating models by transfer, rather than by collinearity screening and within-region
cross-validation alone, gives more reliable models for invasive species [@wenger2012; @dormann2013;
@valavi2022].

## Climatic limits in Australia and New Zealand

The predicted Australian range matches the documented distribution of the tick along the eastern
coast and in Victoria [@hoogstraal1968; @heath2016], and it captures the outlying south-western
Western Australian and north Queensland records. Inland, suitability is limited first by large
diurnal temperature ranges along the western fall of the Great Dividing Range and then by aridity
across the interior. Both reflect the vulnerability of non-feeding stages to desiccation
[@needham1991]. In the tropical north, high mean temperatures limit suitability. Here the native-range
evidence is clear: *H. longicornis* is absent from the tropical lowlands of southern China and
South-East Asia. The few tropical records from Pacific islands come from small, maritime, highly
humid environments that have no counterpart in northern Australia. New Zealand is almost entirely
suitable, consistent with the tick's long-established distribution across the North Island and its
presence in parts of the South Island [@heath2016]. Low annual mean temperature is the main factor
reducing suitability in the south and at altitude.

## Niche conservatism and its implications

The Oceanian niche was equivalent to and more similar than expected to the native niche, with high
stability and limited expansion. This is consistent with the general pattern that climatic niches
are largely conserved during invasion [@petitpierre2012; @guisan2014], and it explains why
native-range information transferred well to Australia and New Zealand. The unfilled part of the
native niche consists of drier, strongly seasonal summer-rainfall climates. In Australia, comparable
rainfall regimes occur mainly in the monsoonal north, where temperatures exceed the species' optimum,
so unfilling probably reflects how climate axes combine in Oceania rather than an inability of the
invasive lineage to tolerate these conditions. The very low overlap with the North
American niche has a different cause. Records there cover a small subset of the available climates,
which is the expected signature of a population still spreading after its detection in 2017
[@rainey2018], rather than a genuine niche shift. Because the North American population is far from
equilibrium, models calibrated only on North American records would greatly underestimate the
species' climatic tolerance. Transfer to East Asia was the weakest in our cross-validation for the
same reason: the invaded ranges sample only part of the native niche. Pooling all three ranges, as
done here, is therefore preferable to calibrating on either native or invaded records alone.

## Implications for surveillance

About `r fmt(100*tot[["gap"]]/tot[["suitable"]], 0)`% of the suitable area lies more than 100 km
from any record in our dataset, mostly in Tasmania, the South Island of New Zealand, western and
coastal Victoria and south-eastern South Australia. These areas are climatically comparable to the
core of the established range, carry large livestock populations, and are connected to infested
regions by stock movements. They are logical targets for structured surveillance. A lack of records
in these areas should not be taken as evidence of absence: our compilation relies on opportunistic
and published records, and some suitable areas may already be occupied but under-reported. Conversely,
surveillance resources are unlikely to be well spent in the arid and tropical interior, where climate
is unsuitable with high confidence and with little extrapolation.

## Limitations

Several limitations should be borne in mind. First, the model describes climatic suitability at a
resolution of about 5 km. It does not account for vegetation, microclimate, host availability
(particularly cattle density) or land use, all of which determine local tick abundance. The binary
maps therefore indicate where populations could persist climatically, not where the tick is present
or abundant. Second, cloglog output is a relative index of suitability, and binary maps depend on
the threshold. The 10th-percentile training-presence threshold is deliberately inclusive of most
known records, but the alternative threshold changes the suitable area (@supptbl-thr). Third, the
target-group data used to correct for sampling bias are themselves uneven, particularly in East
Asia. The close agreement with a uniform background suggests this has little effect on predictions.
Fourth, bisexual and parthenogenetic populations were pooled. The invaded populations are
parthenogenetic, and if the two forms differ in climatic tolerance, the invaded-range niche may be
better represented by the subset of native localities occupied by parthenogenetic populations
[@hoogstraal1968]. Fifth, omission under spatial-block cross-validation (OR10 =
`r fmt(cvs_final$blk_or10)`) was above the nominal 0.10, indicating some residual over-fitting, and
transfer to the native range was weaker than to the invaded ranges. Finally, this analysis addresses
current climate only. Projecting these relationships to future climates will require attention to
extrapolation, because several predictors will move outside the calibration range across northern
and inland Australia [@elith2010; @owens2013].

## Conclusions

The climatic niche of *H. longicornis* has been conserved during its invasion of Australia and
New Zealand, and a model calibrated across all ranges predicts its distribution there accurately,
provided the model includes an absolute temperature gradient and corrects for regional imbalance in
sampling effort. Suitable climate is concentrated on the eastern seaboard of Australia, in Tasmania
and across New Zealand, and is limited inland by aridity and continental temperature regimes. The
climatically suitable but apparently unoccupied areas identified here, especially Tasmania and
southern New Zealand, should be prioritised for surveillance. The transferability-based framework
used here provides a defensible baseline for future projections under climate change.

```{r}
cor_df <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor_bg)) |> mutate(across(1:2, ~ factor(.x, levels = cand_vars)))
ggplot(cor_df, aes(Var1, Var2, fill = Freq)) + geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Freq)), size = 2.3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#b2182b", high = "#2166ac", limits = c(-1, 1), name = "Spearman ρ") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
save_fig("FigS1_predictor_correlation", w = 10, h = 9)
```
Spearman correlations among the `r length(cand_vars)` candidate predictors across the accessible area (evaluation background, n = `r fmt_int(nrow(bg_eval))`).
:::

::: {#suppfig-sens}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6
p_u <- ggplot() + geom_spatraster(data = pred_unif) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, limits = c(0, 1), na.value = NA, name = "Suitability") +
  map_base + labs(tag = "a")
sens_df <- as_tibble(sens_vals) |> setNames(c("bias", "unif")) |> slice_sample(n = 20000)
p_sc <- ggplot(sens_df, aes(bias, unif)) + geom_bin2d(bins = 60) + scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log10", name = "Cells") +
  geom_abline(linetype = 2) + labs(x = "Final model (bias-corrected background)", y = "Uniform background", tag = "b") +
  coord_equal()
p_u + p_sc
save_fig("FigS8_background_sensitivity", p_u + p_sc, 12, 6)
```
Sensitivity to background design. (a) Suitability predicted by the same configuration fitted with a uniform background. (b) Cell-wise comparison with the final model (Spearman ρ = `r fmt(sens_cor)`; binary agreement = `r fmt(100*bin_agree,1)`%). Cross-validated performance with the uniform background: LORO AUC = `r fmt(cv_summary(cv_unif)$loro_auc)`, LORO CBI = `r fmt(cv_summary(cv_unif)$loro_cbi)`, block AUC = `r fmt(cv_summary(cv_unif)$blk_auc)`.
